title: The Leader Is Sometimes the Last to Know
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece explains why leaders often find out about important issues — a struggling team member, a personal crisis, a negative performance trend — later than anyone else in the organization. Team members filter what they share based on what they believe the leader wants to hear, and unless a leader explicitly and repeatedly signals what they want to know about, that filtering quietly excludes important information. The essay frames the fix as straightforward but easy to neglect: leaders must state clearly and often what kinds of information matter to them, treat delayed news as a teaching moment rather than an occasion for blame, and never punish the messenger. It closes by warning that assuming you're getting the information you need is a mistake — you have to actively ask for it.
points: Team members filter what they share based on guesses about what the leader wants to hear.
This filtering means leaders are frequently the last to learn about struggling performance or personal crises.
Leaders who react badly to late news ('killing the messenger') reinforce the filtering problem.
The fix is to repeatedly and explicitly state what kinds of information the leader wants surfaced.
Leaders should treat delayed information as a teaching moment and consistently thank people for sharing it.
quotes: People tend to only share the information they believe the leader wants to hear.
Unless the leader specifically tells people what they want to know about, team members commonly filter many important details, news, and perspectives.
Because leaders assume they will hear about anything “important,” they are often the last to know about critical issues outside of their line of sight.
Good leaders must communicate loudly and repetitively about what they want to know.
Never presume you are getting most of the information you need and desire. You have to ask for it.
